# Sleep Science

## Overview

Rest is the cheapest performance tool I have. Sleep pressure builds the longer I stay awake, driven by adenosine stacking up in the brain; the longer I am up, the stronger the pull toward rest. Once asleep, a night runs in roughly 90-minute cycles, dropping through light sleep, deep sleep and REM before surfacing briefly and starting again. I aim for 7-9 hours, which for most adults means four to six full cycles. Deep sleep handles physical recovery; REM sorts memory and mood. Neither one can be faked, and cutting either short shows up within a few days.

## Sleep Debt

Missing an hour a night adds up quietly. Two weeks of six-hour nights leaves me foggy, slow and hungrier than usual, and a single long lie-in does not clear it. Recovery takes several steady nights, not one. I watch my weekly average rather than judging a single bad night, because one rough night is normal and one good night is not a cure. A short nap helps, but it does not fully repay what is owed; it softens the edge while the balance stays open. The only real cure is a run of ordinary, boring nights with a steady wake time.

## Caffeine

Caffeine blocks adenosine, so it hides pressure rather than clearing it. Its half-life is about five hours, which means half of a 3pm coffee is still working at 8pm and a quarter of it at 1am. I keep the dose small and stop by early afternoon. A 20-minute nap before 2pm works better than a second cup, and it does not wreck the evening. Alcohol is the other trap: it knocks me out fast and then fragments deep sleep, so I keep it light and early.

## Notes

Keep the room cool, dark and quiet. Same wake time every day, weekends included. Morning light and a short walk anchor the rhythm better than any supplement I have tried. If I wake at 3am, I get up rather than lie there fretting. Screen brightness last thing at night is worth cutting, and a paper book is a better landing than a phone. Habits beat gadgets.
